articles.title: Cycling in the wild heart of the Netherlands: an autumnal break in the Veluwe
articles.summary: The untamed, magical landscape takes in a vast national park, palatial houses and a sculpture garden and museum stuffed with Van Goghs – all easily accessible by bike.
body: One minute I’m cycling through an expansive dusty pink stretch of heathland with sloping sand dunes in the distant horizon, the next I’m winding through a fragrant Scots pine forest as sunlight filters through the branches of red-barked trees to make a kaleidoscope of white shapes on the trail floor ahead.

I’m in Hoge Veluwe National Park, a 5,400 hectare (13,000 acre) nature reserve in Gelderland, about an hour and a half from Amsterdam. It’s crisscrossed by 25 miles (40km) of cycling paths, and around 2,000 free-to-use white bikes are available for visitors to explore the ever-changing scenery.

I’ve been flitting back and forth to the Netherlands for years and have lost count of the times friends there have raved about the park and the wider Veluwe region, a forest-rich ridge of hills and diverse landscapes, stretching 37 miles, north to south. Finally I’ve come to see for myself and explore on foot and on two wheels over a few days – adding in a dash of culture at some of its historic towns and museums too.
points: The untamed, magical landscape takes in a vast national park, palatial houses and a sculpture garden and museum stuffed with Van Goghs – all easily accessible by bike.

articles.title: A moment that changed me: I was always a pushover – until I stood up to some teenagers
articles.summary: On the eve of my 40th birthday, I was doused with cold water at a train station. Before, I would have shrugged it off. But suddenly I realised it was time to assert myself.
body: I t was the evening before my 40th birthday – a freezing cold night in March – and I was travelling across London to meet some old school friends for dinner. As I walked down the stairs into the tube station, I spotted a few teens leaning over the balustrade above me. I thought nothing of it; teens hanging about aimlessly is as classic a combination as Archers and lemonade. That was, until they each threw a few KFC paper cups’ worth of icy water over my head.

I noticed it in slow-motion and, at first, kept walking. Then I realised that my hair was wet and so was my back. Without thinking, I ran back up the stairs and followed the teens, who were marching off down the main road. People on the street were watching me, obviously intrigued to see what I was going to do. What was I going to do? A few people looked at me with pity and pointed me in the right direction.

When I caught up with the teenagers, they pretended it wasn’t them. The two girls strode quickly ahead, but one of the boys hung back – perhaps also intrigued to hear what I was going to say. What was I going to say?
points: On the eve of my 40th birthday, I was doused with cold water at a train station.
But suddenly I realised it was time to assert myself.

articles.title: The shocking rise of rib remodelling: ‘I wanted that hourglass shape’
articles.summary: It involves the fracturing of a patient’s ribs, before they spend three months laced into a corset. Some of those who have had this cosmetic procedure say it is like being ‘hit by a bus’. Why is it becoming more popular? Daniela Cesin was 14 when she began thinking about her looks.
body: In August, Cesin travelled from Miami, where she has lived for the past 15 years, to her native Venezuela for liposuction and a fat transfer to her hips. She met her cosmetic surgeon for the first time the day before the procedure, and he realised she didn’t have enough fat to go ahead with it. Instead, he offered to perform RibXcar: a rib remodelling surgery that would involve fracturing three of her lower ribs on each side and binding them in a corset for three months, to set the ribs in a new position and give her a wasplike waist.

“I was like: ‘No, no, no, I don’t want to do anything with the ribs,’” she says. The idea of breaking the bones around her vital organs sounded a lot more invasive than a breast augmentation, which she had 10 years ago, or a rhinoplasty (nose surgery) and blepharoplasty (eyelid surgery), which she had two years ago. Also, she had never heard of the procedure.

articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: to nail this year’s British heritage look, just study Rivals
articles.summary: Thanks to Jilly Cooper, tartan and tweed, waxed jackets and wellies are a style vibe right now. British heritage, in fashion terms, is a country where it is permanently October. A conker-brown and pleasant land, if you will.
body: British heritage is a style vibe right now. Barbour and Mulberry joined Burberry in stepping up to the style plate and taking part in London fashion week this season. Kate Moss is in her wellies for Hunter ’s latest advertising campaign, while Sienna Miller and Idris Elba star in Barbour ’s. Barbour also features a cameo from some sheep, which says something about how countryside-coded the British heritage look is at heart. Fair Isle knits and Argyle diamond-pattern sweaters are worn draped over the shoulders, shown off as trophies. Waxed or tweedy jackets are taking over from urban puffer jackets. The neutral of the season is brown (mud) rather than black (asphalt).

articles.title: Princess Leonor: The Young Spanish Royal Offering a Lesson in Fall Style
articles.summary: Future queen of Spain Princess Leonor is taking a few style cues from her mother, Queen Letizia, while making a case for a fresh and modern royal wardrobe.
body: Princess Leonor of Spain has quite the fashion act to follow. Her mother, Queen Letizia, is one of Europe’s most consistently stylish royals, with a wardrobe that runs the gamut from razor-sharp tailoring and elegant eveningwear to more relaxed, off-duty staples. But the 20-year-old heir to the Spanish throne is steadily establishing a sartorial identity of her own—and, judging by her recent appearances, she's developing a particular knack for fall dressing.

The eldest daughter of King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Leonor de Borbón y Ortiz became first in line to the Spanish throne when her father ascended in 2014. She is the older sister of Infanta Sofía, and granddaughter of former King Juan Carlos I and Queen Sofía. As the Princess of Asturias, Leonor has increasingly taken on a more prominent public role, balancing royal engagements with her military training. And with those growing responsibilities has come an increasingly assured wardrobe, one that mixes Spanish designers, youthful silhouettes, and the occasional piece borrowed from the family jewelry box.
points: Future queen of Spain Princess Leonor is taking a few style cues from her mother, Queen Letizia, while making a case for a fresh and modern royal wardrobe.

articles.title: Kim Kardashian Is Nothing if Not Committed to a Cutout
articles.summary: From Rome to Mexico City, “All’s Fair” star Kim Kardashian is showing some serious skin, and proving that some style signatures are nonnegotiable.
body: Kim Kardashian has never met a cutout she didn’t like. Whether sparkling and sliced into the waist care of custom Erdem, a Gucci gown carved around the hips, or revealing considerably more, strategically placed flashes of skin have long been a Kim Kardashian style signature. And while her new partnership with stylist Law Roach has ushered in a more refined era of archival fashion, some things are simply too good to give up.

Next stop: Mexico City. For the next premiere, Kardashian called upon a longtime favorite of hers—and the wider Kardashian-Jenner family—Schiaparelli. This time, she opted for a look from the house’s latest couture collection: a glossy cream silicone dress with a plunging, tightly fitted halterneck bodice and a skirt constructed from layers of hand-cut fringe, which parted to reveal a delicate, micro-polka-dotted sequin sheer underlayer. Her hair was worn long, slick, and gelled close to the head, keeping all eyes on the dress’s intricate construction and flashes of skin.
points: From Rome to Mexico City, “All’s Fair” star Kim Kardashian is showing some serious skin, and proving that some style signatures are nonnegotiable.

articles.title: Why You Might Find Yourself Fishing, Foraging—Or Even Hunting—On Your Next Vacation
articles.summary: Some luxury travelers don't want to lift a finger. Others want dirt in their fingernails and fish guts on their hands.
body: There are two types of luxury hotels these days: Those where you don’t have to lift a finger. And those where you might find yourself elbow-deep in the cavity of an elk that you, of all people, just harvested. As in: stalked, shot, and gutted, and butchered.

Whatever you’re doing, if you’re a food-obsessed traveler in 2027, you may find yourself foraging, fishing, or even hunting on your next trip. Call it the next iteration of farm-to-table—but one thing is clear: The hospitality industry has officially gone wild.

At some of the world’s most exclusive hotels, old-world service is giving way to old-world skills. The kind most urban-dwelling, laptop-pecking, Door Dash-ordering professionals have lost. And are looking to gain... on vacation.

articles.title: The Kitchen Gear That's Topped Our ‘Best Of’ Lists for a Decade
articles.summary: You won't find better tools than these—trust us, we've tried.
body: A deluge of feature-laden, Wi-Fi connected, “revolutionary” new cooking products come out every year, yet there are some kitchen necessities that just can’t be improved upon. Believe us: At BA, we’ve been testing products head-to-head to find the best cookware, tools, and appliances since 2015, and during that decade, our editors have returned to a small handful of favorites time and again.

With boxes full of kitchen gear arriving at the office practically every single day for our team of kitchen obsessives to put through the wringer, the odds are stacked against any particular item finding a stable spot as a favorite. Yet, here we are, with a list of 15 timeless pieces that reached the top of our rankings and just…stayed there.

As part of our Gear of the Year Awards, we're continuing to recognize this core group of products—selected by our Test Kitchen editors and reviews team—as our Forever Award winners. Invest in these, and you can feel confident that they won't soon be bested.

articles.title: Learning to Hunt Pheasant at an All-Women Retreat in South Dakota
articles.summary: In shooting and harvesting her own dinner, writer Heide Brandes finds community—and reverence—among the sorghum fields of South Dakota.
body: The sorghum hissed when the wind came through it—two years of drought had left the South Dakota ground hard and the dry grass loud. I walked forwards with my 20-gauge Beretta half-raised and my eyes narrowed; the sound of every grasshopper that clattered up out of the stubble made me twitch like a woman with a bad nerve.
Then the pheasant rooster came up, multicolored and shining in the sun, trailing a tail of feathers like a kite. I aimed, let loose the shot, and it stopped dead in the air in an iridescent burst.

The pride went through me before anything else did. The tears came second, running unexpectedly down my face while a dozen women I had only known for two days hollered happily for me. Laying the rooster across my arm, I petted him and told him I was sorry.

articles.title: More Pieces, More Possibilities: How to Merchandise Maximalism
articles.summary: The brands that offer uniform-building wardrobes that go beyond the minimalist days of yore — in line with this season’s ‘messy girl’ trend — will win.
body: This season, even quiet luxury all-timer The Row showed gorgeous, beaded, colorful tops, while the stark whites and creams that still dominated the collection were paired with chunky beaded necklaces and lace and crochet detailing.

It’s a signal of the balance fashion brands now need to strike between the minimalism of the past five years and the maximalism this season was heralded for bringing back. Almost every buyer’s takeaway this season was that the collections offered looks that were deconstructable; pieces that are easy to wear and pair together (or apart), without being overly prescribed. Looks are buildable, pieces interchangeable — and the best ones had an edge.

articles.title: At Celine, CEO Séverine Merle Is Taking Things One Triomphe at a Time
articles.summary: The Celine CEO shares her strategy for growing desirability at a difficult time for luxury.
body: See all that bright red and blue showing up in clothes everywhere? You can probably thank Celine’s Michael Rider for that, and for the flocks of red sweaters draped over shoulders on city streets from Paris to New York. On the runway, too, the excitement around the designer’s individualized approach to dressing ( and those disc-shaped glasses ) is felt. Even the red carpet is reaping the benefit; just take Carey Mulligan’s pleated silver gown, for instance.
It’s clear that Rider is doing something increasingly tricky for luxury today: creating products that people truly want.

“We need to keep building on that desirability. It’s very strong, as you can see from the press coverage,” Celine CEO Séverine Merle says, speaking from her office at the brand’s HQ, housed within Paris’s Hôtel Colbert de Torcy. She herself is wearing the brand’s Heirloom necklace, featuring an array of charms.
points: The Celine CEO shares her strategy for growing desirability at a difficult time for luxury.
